newsitem.title: GERMANY: Yeltsin says NATO-Russia deal will be signed in May.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says NATO-Russia deal will be signed in May.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin said on Thursday after a summit with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl that an agreement governing Russia's relations with an expanding NATO would be signed in May.

Yeltsin, looking waxen-faced and tired, told reporters he and Kohl had been in broad agreement on the thorny problem, intended to help allay Russia's emphatic objections to NATO's planned inclusion of eastern European countries.

"We want to announce that...on the 27th of May in Paris an agreement will be signed by the leaders of the NATO countries and of Russia," Yeltsin said, before making clear that much discussion remained by adding "So we'll have to hurry".

On the eve of the talks, Yeltsin's spokesman had taken a cooler tone, warning that Moscow still saw NATO expansion as the West's "biggest mistake since the Cold War" and that Russia would not sign a deal without getting the guarantees it wants.

The meeting was the fifth between the two men since the start of last year, and both were at pains to stress the personal friendship which has become an important tool in easing strain in relations between Russia and the West.

Kohl chose to receive Yeltsin in the stately spa town of Baden-Baden, famed in the last century as the "summer capital" of Europe's nobility, not least Russian tsars and writers, and home to a host of private clinics and the casino immortalised in Fyodor Dostoyevsky's 1860s novel "The Gambler".

Yeltsin, 66 and back in action for only a couple of months after a long illness, looked tired at the end of the day of talks. While Kohl addressed a joint news conference after lunch at a country restaurant, Yeltsin stared stonily ahead.
Kohl said he hoped a deal on NATO could be struck next month, helped by the good offices of Germany. But he also made more of the obstacles ahead.

"I am confident that, with good will on both sides, we can come to an agreement before the NATO-Russia summit on May 27," Kohl said. He noted however that, while four chapters of the treaty were "90 percent" complete, a fifth, dealing with nuts and bolts military issues, posed significant problems.
"It still needs a lot of work but I see good chances."
Russian is demanding NATO agree to limit the stationing of foreign troops in East European countries that join the alliance have held up preparations for the planned May 27 summit.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said on Wednesday the negotiations might not be finished in time for the meeting.
Yeltsin repeated Russia's insistence on a say in NATO decision-making through consensus and that nuclear and other weapons not be deployed closer to Russia's borders.
NATO leaders, especially the United States, are unwilling to give such sweeping undertakings that would consign new members like Poland and Hungary to "second-class" NATO participation.

Peppering their news conference with "dear Boris" and "my friend Helmut", the two men said they had also made progress in settling a long dispute over German art treasures seized by the Soviet Army after World War Two.

There would be no quick solution but in a gesture of goodwill Yeltsin brought Kohl a collection of papers of the 1922 German foreign minister Walther Rathenau and announced he had ordered the release to Germany of copies of the East German communist party records held in Moscow since the 1970s.

Yeltsin was due to recieve a "Man of the Year" award from the German media on Thursday night and to fly back to Russia on Friday morning -- possibly directly to the Black Sea resort of Sochi where he is due to spend a few days holiday.
